newsitem.title: MEXICO: Calm elections catapult Mexico shrs to new record.
newsitem.headline: Calm elections catapult Mexico shrs to new record.

text.p: The Mexican bourse soared to its fifth record close in a row Monday as domestic and foreign investors drew confidence from Sunday's mid-term elections being relatively free of fraud allegations that have tarnished polls in the past, dealers said.
"The most important event of the year is now behind us with no major casualties," said Gordon Lee, an equity analyst with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell-Mexico.
Final closing prices placed the blue chip IPC index was up 96.70 points on the day, or 2.08 percent, at a new record of 4,741.30.

"The fact that the parties recognised each others' victories, and the speed and extent of that recognition was a very mature response," Lee added. "There was something for everybody in this election."
Mexicans voted on Sunday to renew the entire lower chamber of Congress, one quarter of the Senate, several state governors and, for the first time in modern Mexico, a mayor for the capital.
A preliminary count showed Cuauhtmoc Crdenas, of the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) with a 22-point lead in the historic Mexico City race.
President Ernesto Zedillo, of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), congratulated Crdenas on Sunday night.
Early returns also showed the conservative National Action Party had wrested control of two states from the PRI.
The PRI was meanwhile heading to lose its overall majority in the lower house, but was still the largest single party and may have retained at least two states.
For Lars Schonander, research head at Santander Investment-Mexico, the Mexican bourse was moving under its own steam after clearing the hurdle of post-electoral violence.
"The bourse is still climbing as it has lagged other LatAm markets. Now it has decoupled from the elections, we also have lower interest rates in the offing," he said.
Lee added post-electoral calm helped the bourse shrug off a slide of 37.32 points on the Dow Jones, which closed at 7,858.49.
Dealers said blue chips drove the market, notably from the financial sector.
"As there were relatively few post-electoral problems, the outlook for domestic interest rates is downward," said Enrique Pani, a banking analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell-Mexico.
"And that alleviates past-due loans burdens for banks in general," he added.

Bancomer, one of Mexico's biggest financial groups, gained 40 centavos to 4.42 pesos. The group's A and B shares together accounted for almost one quarter of all shares traded, dealers said, on heavy foreign demand.

Market heavyweight Telfonos de Mxico (Telmex) leaped 70 centavos to a record close in peso terms of 20.60 pesos. The telecom's ADRs meanwhile climbed 2-1/8 to 51-7/8, their highest level since the December 1994 peso crisis.
Dealers also drew attention to gains by building firm Empresas ICA and cement maker Cemex, both market heavyweights.

"They're very liquid stocks which absorb market liquidity," Lee said, adding ICA was a laggard that had also benefitted from market forecasts of a government plan to restructure debts for highway concessionaires.
Cemex was gaining ahead of an expected improvement in second quarter earnings, Lee added.
ICA gained 5.70 pesos to 141.50 pesos, while Cemex was up 55 centavos to 36.50 pesos.
Trading volume was heavy at 142.6 million shares.
The broad market mirrored buoyant blue chips, with gainers outnumbering sliders by 81 to 22 out of a total of 127 stocks that changed hands.
(( -- Martin Roberts, Mexico City newsroom +525 728-7907))
